title: Against Resolutions
author: Suleika Jaouad
summary: Suleika Jaouad challenges the cultural mythology of New Year's resolutions, arguing they fail structurally because they depend on willpower (a finite, depletable resource) and promise binary outcomes (success or failure), neither of which aligns with how humans actually change. Research shows most resolutions collapse within a month, leaving people not renewed but quietly demoralized. Jaouad proposes an alternative framework: rituals instead of resolutions. Unlike outcome-driven resolutions, rituals are relational, process-focused, and gentler—they create rhythm and containment without demanding performance transformation. Drawing on artists like Georgia O'Keeffe and designer Michael Bierut, the 100-Day Project demonstrates rituals in action: by reducing the question from 'Can I complete this for a year?' to 'Can I show up today?' The scaffold of ritual allows messy, unedited work within simple containers, keeping people in motion without forcing a chokehold on results.
points: Resolutions fail structurally: they depend on willpower (a finite resource that depletes under stress) and demand binary outcomes, creating inevitable failure states that demoralize rather than motivate.
Research shows most resolutions fail within a month, beginning the year not with renewal but with quiet shame; the resolution framework itself—not human weakness—is the problem.

Rituals differ fundamentally from resolutions in that they are relational, process-oriented, and focused on attending to practice rather than demanding performance; they create rhythm and containment without hardening against failure.

The 100-Day Project shows how reframing the question from 'Can I do this for a year?' to 'Can I do this today?' removes the cliff effect and enables consistent participation without the performance pressure of resolutions.

Rituals create simple containers that make room for mess and editing; they steady the practitioner, open possibility without demanding transformation, and accumulate sustainable change through daily attendance rather than willpower.
